| [NOTE-100](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-100.md) v2 | Bourrat — Reproducees, reproducers, Darwinian individuals | Bourrat builds a nested vocabulary. A reproducee is a B that comes after A, is caused by A, and is of A's relevant class. A reproducer is a reproducee with reproductive autonomy, meaning it can reproduce across a range of backgrounds. A Darwinian individual is a reproducer with high reproductive causal control, meaning heredity survives as the parent's description is made finer. On that vocabulary, genes of multicellular organisms are, like hearts, mere reproducees, but with high control. Material overlap is necessary for reproducers, which are whole life cycles, and unnecessary for reproducees, so Griesemer and Godfrey-Smith partly talk past each other. Both quantities get an information-theoretic recipe (conditional MI after Bertschinger et al. 2008 for autonomy; interventional MI across grains, Griffiths et al.'s INF, for control), and neither is computed. | Read |

| [NOTE-124](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-124.md) v2 | McKenzie — Emergence from physics to computer science | Sole-authored survey by a condensed-matter physicist. It takes novelty (a property the parts lack) as the defining mark of emergence and sets it against twelve other characteristics in §2. The six "objective" ones are discontinuities, order, modification of parts, universality, diversity and mesoscale modularity. The six "subjective" ones are self-organisation, unpredictability, irreducibility, contextuality/downward causation, complexity and intra-stratum closure. Case studies from the Ising model to Schelling segregation and LLMs show that each can come apart from novelty: novelty without discontinuity (Kondo, Fermi liquids, spin ice), without unpredictability (BKT, spin ice), and with reduction (Butterfield). §22 sides with weak emergence and argues that strong-emergence claims from molecular structure are weak. | Read |
| [NOTE-126](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-126.md) v2 | Worrall — Evidence in medicine and EBM | Worrall argues that the EBM evidence hierarchy has no sound general rationale for giving randomisation extra epistemic weight, even though it lets high-quality RCTs "trump any number of observational studies". He examines five standard arguments. Four fail: (a) Fisher's significance-test logic, (b) control of unknown confounders, (d) that observational studies "exaggerate" effects, and (e) probabilistic causality. The fifth, (c) selection bias, is a "cast-iron argument", but it supports only taking allocation out of the clinicians' hands, and randomisation is one way to do that. What matters is balance on plausible confounders, a placebo or active control and blinding. Whether balance comes from randomising or from matching "seems epistemically unimportant", and historically controlled trials can give strong evidence for large effects. | Read |
| [NOTE-137](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-137.md) v2 | Hazelwood — Emerging dilemma for reciprocal causation | Hazelwood defines RC as "the process of natural selection is both a cause and effect of processes such as niche construction" and EC as "natural selection is an emergent causal process". If EC holds, niche construction partly composes selection, so the two fail Woodward's independent-fixability condition and cannot stand in a causal relation. | [NOTE-155](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-155.md) v2 | Trappes — Defining the niche for niche construction | Trappes compares NCT's evolutionary niche with the ecological niche. The evolutionary niche is the sum of selection pressures on a population (Odling-Smee, Laland & Feldman 2003), read "externally" as the environmental factors that produce fitness differences. The ecological niche is the conditions that permit continued existence; for a population, mean absolute fitness ≥ 1. Even at their closest, against the realized population niche, the two differ in extension. Habitat degradation is in the evolutionary niche but not the ecological one, and commensalism and non-limiting resources are in the ecological niche but not the evolutionary one. So NCT's niche is not the "simple translation" of Hutchinson's niche its proponents claim, and the evolutionary significance of niche construction must be shown case by case rather than following from the definition. | Read |

| [NOTE-173](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-173.md) v2 | Griesemer & Shavit — Scaffolding individuality (3Cs) | The paper sets out an idealized three-stage sequence of interaction types, which it calls a "first and rough sketch" (§1). Stage 1 is coordination in *collections* (pairwise, "aggregative" interactions of co-located individuals). Stage 2 is cooperation in *conexuses* (a connected web of binary interactions whose benefits can still be counted per member). Stage 3 is collaboration in *communities*: heterogeneous multi-way interactions around a shared goal, in which generatively entrenched "core" interactions give organizational closure. Table 1 puts the transition to a new level of individuality between stages 2 and 3 only. The paper asserts, rather than argues, that this describes evolutionary transitions non-circularly and that individuality is a special case of collectivity. | [NOTE-310](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-310.md) | Notes on Landauer's principle, reversible computation, and Maxwell's Demon | Bennett states Landauer's principle as a consequence of the Second Law. A logically irreversible step, meaning erasure or a *merge of control flow*, must export at least the lost entropy (k ln 2 per bit) to non-information-bearing degrees of freedom. That export need not take the form of heat (p. 1). Logically reversible operations, including copying onto a blank register and measurement, have no minimum cost. He calls "an intrinsic cost of order kT for every elementary act of information processing" a 20th-century "misconception" (pp. 5–6). Erasing random data can itself be thermodynamically reversible; the waste comes from applying a many-to-one operation to *known* data (pp. 1, 4). | Read |
| [NOTE-330](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-330.md) | Damasio & Carvalho — The nature of feelings | An Opinion with no new data. Feelings are the felt side of interoceptive body maps, and they report homeostatic value. Feeling does not need the insula: the authors' own patient with both insulae destroyed still feels. It needs the upper brainstem, where whole-body maps first assemble. The evolutionary story (felt maps beat unfelt ones because they support learning and anticipation) and the cellular one (unmyelinated, ligand- and ion-permeable interoceptive axons, with ephaptic coupling, as the root of sentience) are hypotheses, and are presented as such. | Read |
